title: Magnetosphere and changing fields
target: Use evidence to distinguish a magnetic-field model from an unsupported space-weather claim.
criteria: Connect changing magnetic fields with induced electric effects.
Distinguish an assumption from an observation.
Name evidence required for a space-weather prediction.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A changing external magnetic field passes through a conducting loop. Which mechanism could produce an electrical effect?
options: Magnetic fields are identical to gravitational fields.
Constant magnetic flux always consumes charge.
Changing flux can induce emf in the loop.
The loop must directly touch the source.
cpa.guide: Faraday induction can link changing magnetic conditions to electrical effects.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: In a coil model, tripling the flux-change rate triples induced emf when other conditions are fixed. If the original magnitude is 1.5 V, what is the new magnitude?
cpa.guide: Emf magnitude is proportional to flux-change rate for the same coil.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A model assumes an Earth field is uniform across a loop. Which observation would directly challenge that assumption?
options: The model uses the word uniform.
Measurements show substantially different field strengths at opposite sides of the loop.
The loop has a familiar shape.
One measurement was taken somewhere else last year.
cpa.guide: Spatial variation across the actual modeled loop challenges uniformity there.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: A report says “a voltage pulse was measured” and “the pulse was caused by a particular space event.” Which distinction is correct?
options: Neither could ever be tested.
A measured voltage uniquely identifies any remote cause.
Both statements are automatically direct observations.
The measured pulse is evidence; the proposed cause needs additional supporting evidence.
cpa.guide: An electrical observation does not by itself establish a unique external cause.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: Which data would help assess an induction-based space-weather prediction for a long circuit?
options: Time-varying magnetic measurements plus the circuit geometry and electrical properties.
Only a dramatic headline.
Only a single constant field value with no time information.
Only the circuit’s paint color.
cpa.guide: Induction depends on change, geometry, and response of the receiving system.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A simplified model predicts a voltage pulse but omits shielding and circuit response. What claim is justified?
options: It suggests a possible induced effect, but cannot by itself determine actual equipment damage.
All equipment will certainly fail.
Model uncertainty proves no field change occurred.
All equipment will certainly be safe.
cpa.guide: Real consequences require coupling, protection, and device-response evidence beyond the simplified prediction.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
